4.text: VOLUNTARY DEATH. — Voluntary death is still of frequent occurrence

5.text: among the Chukchee. It is inflicted by a friend or relative, upon the expressed

6.text: wish of the person who desires to die. Though I had no occasion to witness

7.text: a case of voluntary death, I know of about twenty cases which happened

8.text: among the Chukchee during the time of my travels. One summer, while I

9.text: was at Mariinsky Post, a large skin boat from the Telqäˊp tundra arrived for

10.text: trading-purposes. One of the new-comers, after a visit to the Russian bar-

11.text: racks, felt a sudden pain in his stomach. During the night the pain became

12.text: acute, the sufferer asked to be killed, and his fellow-travellers complied with

14.text: From what has been related, it will be seen that the voluntary death of

15.text: old men is not prompted by any lack of good feeling towards the old men,

16.text: but rather by the hard conditions of their life, which make existence almost

17.text: unendurable for any one unable to take full care of himself. Accordingly,

18.text: not only old people, but also those afflicted by some illness, often prefer death

19.text: to continued suffering; and their number is even greater than that of old

20.text: people who die a voluntary death.

21.text: The position of an infirm man among the Chukchee is very hard indeed,

22.text: be he young or old. On the western Kolyma tundra I met a man less than

23.text: thirty years of age, Aˊnɪqai by name, who three years before was stricken

24.text: with palsy, and, though partly recovered, had become feeble-minded. I saw

25.text: him in February. It was cold and windy. The Chukchee of the western

26.text: Kolyma tundra have no winter houses, and wander about throughout the year

27.text: with their usual travelling-tent and sleeping-room. Thus did also the family

28.text: of Aˊnɪqai. We visited them at a newly chosen camping-place. The women

29.text: had just begun to unload the pack-sledges. The tent could be pitched only

30.text: late in the evening. Aˊnɪqai lay on the snow, looking very much like a heap

31.text: of old clothes. His wife put a clothing-bag under his head; but, the bag

32.text: being short and round, his head almost immediately fell to the ground again.

33.text: His cap also had fallen off, and the wind began to fill his hair with fine dry

34.text: snow. The cold was so severe that even the Chukchee could keep warm

35.text: only by continual exercise. Aˊnɪqai lay there quite motionless. I caught his

36.text: look. Though dull and feeble, it was full of helpless pain, and had something

37.text: of that of a dying animal.

38.text: Another tragic figure of my acquaintance was a woman of forty, who

39.text: suffered from lung trouble, and whom I saw on the Dry Anui River when

40.text: I had to spend a couple of days in her camp. She had been very active in

41.text: her youth, a good “shaker of the tent,” as the Chukchee say. Even at that
